dock-docker.md:
## Why it exists
'It works on my machine' used to be a daily argument: different OS versions, libraries and runtimes. A **container** packages an app with everything it needs and runs it as an isolated process on any machine with a container runtime. Unlike a virtual machine, it shares the host kernel, so it starts in milliseconds and uses a fraction of the memory.

{{dg:0}}

Mental model: an image is a recipe frozen into a stack of read-only layers; a container is one running instance of it. Isolation comes from Linux features (namespaces limit what a process can see, cgroups limit what it can use), not from a separate OS.

## Core vocabulary
- **Docker image:** immutable, layered filesystem plus metadata (command, environment). Identified by tag (`node:22-slim`) or immutable **image digest** (`sha256:...`).
- **Registry:** where images live (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, ECR, ACR).
- **Volume:** storage that outlives a container. Anything written in the container's own layer disappears when it is removed.
- **Network:** containers on the same network reach each other by service name.

## Worked example: a production Dockerfile for a Node API
{{dg:1}}
```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci

FROM deps AS build
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

FROM node:22-slim AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production
WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build --chown=app:app /app/dist ./dist
COPY --chown=app:app package.json ./
USER app
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD node -e 'fetch("http://localhost:3000/healthz").then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))'
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```
What each choice buys you:
- **Multi-stage build:** compilers and dev dependencies stay in the build stage; the runtime image holds only what runs. Smaller, faster to pull, smaller attack surface.
- **Copy the lockfile first:** the dependency layer is rebuilt only when dependencies change, not on every code edit.
- **Non-root user:** a compromised app does not own the container.
- **Exec-form CMD** (JSON array): Node is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly, so it can shut down gracefully. Shell form wraps it in `sh` and swallows signals.
- **HEALTHCHECK** lets Docker and Compose know when the app, not just the process, is ready.
Add a `.dockerignore` with `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env*`, `dist` and logs so secrets and junk never enter the build context.

## Commands you use daily
```bash
docker build -t api:dev .                     # build an image from the Dockerfile
docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env.local api:dev
docker ps                                     # running containers
docker logs -f <container>                    # follow logs
docker exec -it <container> sh                # shell into a running container
docker image ls && docker system df           # sizes and disk usage
docker system prune                           # reclaim space (read what it deletes)
```

## Docker Compose for local development
**Docker Compose** describes a multi-container app in one file:
```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ['3000:3000']
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:app@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }   # wait until Postgres actually accepts connections
  db:
    image: postgres:17
    environment: { POSTGRES_USER: app, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: app, POSTGRES_DB: app }
    healthcheck:
      test: ['CMD-SHELL', 'pg_isready -U app']
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10
    volumes: ['pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data']
volumes:
  pgdata: {}
```
`docker compose up --build` starts both; `docker compose down -v` also deletes the data volume. The `db` hostname resolves because Compose creates a network where service names are DNS names.

## Hardening checklist
| Practice | Why |
|---|---|
| Non-root user, `--read-only` filesystem, `--cap-drop ALL`, `no-new-privileges` | Limits what a compromised process can do |
| Small base (slim, distroless, Alpine where musl is fine) | Fewer packages, fewer CVEs |
| Pin base images by digest in production | Tags move; digests do not |
| Scan images (Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout) in CI | Catch known CVEs before deploy |
| No secrets in `ENV`, `ARG` or layers; use BuildKit secret mounts or runtime injection | Layers are readable by anyone with the image |
| Rebuild regularly | Base-image patches only arrive when you rebuild |
| Never mount the Docker socket into a container | Equivalent to root on the host |

A BuildKit secret mount keeps a token out of the final image:
```dockerfile
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npm_token NPM_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/npm_token) npm ci
```
built with `docker build --secret id=npm_token,env=NPM_TOKEN .`

## In real products
- CI builds an image per commit, tags it with the git SHA, scans it, pushes it to a registry, and the platform (ECS, Cloud Run, Container Apps, Kubernetes) pulls and runs that exact image: the same artifact in staging and production.
- Local dev uses Compose for databases and queues; devcontainers give every teammate the same toolchain.
- Containers are for stateless processes; data lives in managed databases or mounted volumes.

> [!pitfall] `COPY . .` before installing dependencies. Every code edit invalidates the dependency layer and every build takes minutes.
> [!pitfall] Using the `latest` tag. You cannot tell what is running or reproduce a rollback.
> [!pitfall] Writing logs and uploads to the container filesystem. Log to stdout and use object storage or volumes for files.
> [!security] Build arguments and environment variables are visible with `docker history` and `docker inspect`. Treat any secret baked into an image as public.
> [!tip] Handle SIGTERM in your app: stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, then exit. Orchestrators send SIGTERM before SIGKILL.
> [!cost] Image size is egress and cold-start time. A 1.2 GB image on a serverless platform costs real seconds per cold start.
q: How is a container different from a virtual machine?
A container is an isolated process sharing the host kernel, so it is lighter and starts faster; a VM runs a full guest OS on virtualized hardware.
Why copy package.json and the lockfile before the rest of the source?
So the dependency-install layer stays cached until dependencies change, instead of rebuilding on every code edit.
Why use the exec form of CMD?
The app runs as PID 1 and receives termination signals directly, allowing graceful shutdown.
Why is putting a secret in an ARG or ENV in the Dockerfile unsafe?
It is stored in image metadata or layers and can be read by anyone who can pull the image.
res: Official guidance on layers, caching and multi-stage builds
Passing secrets at build time without baking them in

## Why it exists
One container on one machine is easy. Running dozens of services on many machines is not: who restarts a crashed process, spreads load, rolls out a new version without downtime, or reschedules work when a server dies? **Kubernetes** (K8s) is an orchestrator that does this. You tell it what you want ('three copies of this image, reachable on this name') and it continuously works to make reality match.

{{dg:0}}

Mental model: a thermostat, not a script. You set the desired state; control loops compare it to the actual state and act on the difference, forever.

## Architecture in two minutes
- **Control plane:** the API server (the only front door; everything goes through it), etcd (the database of cluster state), the scheduler (picks a node for each Pod) and controller managers (the reconcile loops).
- **Worker nodes:** the kubelet (agent that starts containers), a container runtime (containerd) and networking (kube-proxy or an eBPF CNI like Cilium).
- Managed services (EKS, AKS, GKE) run the control plane for you. You pay and operate the nodes, or use serverless nodes (Fargate, Autopilot).

## The objects that matter
| Object | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Kubernetes Pod** | Smallest unit: one or more containers sharing network and storage. Disposable; never treat it as a pet. |
| **Kubernetes Deployment** | Keeps N identical Pods running and performs rolling updates and rollbacks |
| **Kubernetes Service** | Stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of Pods (selected by labels) |
| **Kubernetes Ingress** / Gateway API | Routes external HTTP(S) traffic to Services |
| ConfigMap / Secret | Non-sensitive config and sensitive values injected as env or files |
| Namespace | Logical partition for teams, environments and quotas |
| StatefulSet, Job, CronJob | Ordered stateful workloads, run-to-completion tasks, scheduled tasks |

## Worked example: a production-shaped Deployment
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  strategy: { rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 } }   # never drop below 3 ready Pods
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: api } }
    spec:
      securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, seccompProfile: { type: RuntimeDefault } }
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:IMAGE_DIGEST          # pinned artifact from CI
          ports: [{ containerPort: 3000 }]
          envFrom: [{ secretRef: { name: api-secrets } }]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }               # what the scheduler reserves
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }                            # exceeding memory gets the Pod OOM-killed
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 3000 }, periodSeconds: 5 }
          livenessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 3000 }, initialDelaySeconds: 10, periodSeconds: 10 }
          securityContext: { allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities: { drop: [ALL] } }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  selector: { app: api }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 3000 }]
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api }
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 } }
```
{{dg:1}}

## Probes and resources: the two settings that cause most outages
- **Readiness probe:** decides whether a Pod receives traffic. Failing it removes the Pod from the Service without restarting it. Use it for 'dependencies are connected and I can serve'.
- **Liveness probe:** decides whether to restart the container. Keep it cheap and independent of dependencies; if it checks the database, a database blip restarts every Pod at once and turns a small incident into a large one.
- **Startup probe** protects slow-starting apps from being killed by liveness during boot.
- **Requests** are what the scheduler reserves; **limits** are the ceiling. A common pattern: set CPU requests but no CPU limit (CPU limits throttle), and set memory requests equal to memory limits so behavior is predictable.
- The **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler** scales replicas on metrics like CPU; it needs requests set to compute utilization.

## Rollouts and debugging
```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/                         # declare desired state
kubectl rollout status deployment/api         # wait for the rollout
kubectl rollout undo deployment/api           # roll back to the previous ReplicaSet
kubectl get pods -l app=api -o wide           # state, restarts, node
kubectl describe pod <pod>                    # events: ImagePullBackOff, OOMKilled, failed probes
kubectl logs <pod> --previous                 # logs of the crashed prior container
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh                  # shell in
kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80          # reach a Service locally
kubectl top pods                              # CPU and memory (needs metrics-server)
```
Common failure words and their meaning: `CrashLoopBackOff` (the process keeps exiting; read `logs --previous`), `ImagePullBackOff` (wrong tag or registry credentials), `Pending` (no node fits the requests), `OOMKilled` (memory limit exceeded).

## Security essentials
- Run workloads as non-root with a restricted **Pod Security Standard** (enforced by the built-in Pod Security Admission via namespace labels).
- **Kubernetes RBAC:** give each workload its own ServiceAccount with only the verbs it needs; never mount cluster-admin into an app. Disable token auto-mount when not needed.
- **NetworkPolicy:** by default every Pod can reach every Pod. Add a default-deny policy per namespace and allow only required flows (requires a CNI that enforces policies).
- Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted, unless you enable encryption at rest. Prefer an external store (External Secrets Operator, the Secrets Store CSI driver with Key Vault or Secrets Manager).
- Pin images by digest, scan them, and verify signatures at admission (Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller).

## Packaging and delivery
Plain YAML grows repetitive. **Helm** templates charts with per-environment values; Kustomize overlays patch base manifests. GitOps tools (Argo CD, Flux) watch a Git repository and sync the cluster to it, so deploys are pull requests and every change is audited.

## When to use it, and when not to
| Situation | Better fit |
|---|---|
| One or a few stateless services, small team | Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, Azure Container Apps, Vercel, Fly.io |
| Many services, custom networking, multi-cloud or on-premises, platform team available | Kubernetes |
| Scheduled batch with spiky load | Serverless functions or jobs |
Kubernetes buys flexibility with real operational weight: upgrades every few months, networking, security and cost tuning. Most small products are better served by a managed container platform until they outgrow it.

## In real products
- Companies run a platform layer on top (ingress controller, cert-manager, external-dns, observability with Prometheus and OpenTelemetry) so product teams only write a Deployment.
- Upgrade discipline matters: the project releases a new minor version about every four months, and managed offerings retire old ones on a schedule, so plan upgrade windows.
- The ingress-nginx controller was announced for retirement in 2026; new clusters increasingly use the Gateway API or a vendor controller.

> [!pitfall] No resource requests: the scheduler packs everything on one node, then neighbors starve each other.
> [!pitfall] A liveness probe that depends on the database. One outage restarts everything.
> [!pitfall] Using the latest tag with imagePullPolicy defaults. Different nodes can run different code.
> [!security] Any Pod that can reach the Kubernetes API with a powerful token is a path to the whole cluster. Scope ServiceAccounts tightly.
> [!cost] Over-requested CPU and memory is the main waste; right-size with real usage data and use cluster autoscaling.
> [!prod] Set PodDisruptionBudgets and spread replicas across zones with topology spread constraints so node drains and zone failures do not take the service down.
q: What does 'desired state' mean in Kubernetes?
You declare what should exist (image, replicas, config) and controllers continuously reconcile the cluster toward it, restarting or rescheduling as needed.
How do readiness and liveness probes differ?
Readiness controls whether a Pod receives traffic; liveness decides whether the container is restarted.
Why is a liveness probe that checks the database dangerous?
A database outage would fail every Pod's liveness check and restart them all, amplifying the incident.
Is a Kubernetes Secret encrypted by default?
No, it is only base64-encoded; enable encryption at rest or use an external secret store.

k8s-production.md:
## Why it exists
The first Kubernetes lesson got a Pod running and exposed. Production is a different problem: a node dies at 3 a.m., a deploy drops requests, one noisy workload starves another, a database loses its disk, or a leaked token reads every Secret. This lesson covers the settings that decide whether the cluster degrades gracefully.

{{dg:0}}

## Requests, limits and QoS
- **Requests** are what the scheduler reserves for the Pod. **Limits** are the ceiling enforced at runtime.
- Exceeding a **memory limit** kills the container (OOMKilled, exit code 137). Exceeding a **CPU limit** only throttles it, which shows up as mysterious latency.
- The **QoS class** follows from your settings. **Guaranteed** (requests equal limits for every container), **Burstable** (some requests set), **BestEffort** (none). Under node memory pressure BestEffort Pods are evicted first.
- A common production pattern: set memory request equal to memory limit (predictable, no surprise OOM from neighbours) and set a CPU request but consider no CPU limit, so Pods can use idle cores. Teams disagree on this; measure throttling (`container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total`) before choosing.
- Size from data: start from observed p95 usage with Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommendations or your metrics. Requests set too high waste money; too low causes noisy-neighbour trouble. Since Kubernetes 1.35, **in-place Pod resize** is stable, so CPU and memory can often be changed on a running Pod without a restart.

## Scheduling: where Pods land
- **nodeSelector and node affinity:** require or prefer nodes with labels (GPU, instance type).
- **Taints and tolerations:** nodes repel Pods unless the Pod tolerates the taint. Use them to reserve nodes for GPUs or system workloads.
- **Pod anti-affinity and topology spread constraints:** spread replicas across zones and nodes so one failure does not take all of them. `topologySpreadConstraints` with `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` is the modern default.
- **Priority classes:** let critical Pods preempt low-priority ones when the cluster is full.

## Staying up during change
- **Rolling updates:** `maxUnavailable: 0` with `maxSurge: 1` adds a new Pod before removing an old one.
- **Probes:** readiness controls whether a Pod receives traffic; liveness restarts a wedged container; startup gives slow apps time before liveness begins. A liveness probe that checks a database will restart every Pod when the database blips.
- **Graceful shutdown:** on termination Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, but endpoints are removed asynchronously. A short `preStop` sleep plus an app that stops accepting new work and drains (and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` longer than your longest request) prevents dropped requests during deploys.
- **PodDisruptionBudget (PDB):** limits how many replicas can be voluntarily evicted at once (node drains, upgrades, autoscaler scale-down). Without one, a cluster upgrade can drain every replica of a service together.
- **Native sidecars:** a sidecar is an init container with `restartPolicy: Always`. It starts before your app, runs alongside it, and shuts down after it; this fixes the old log-shipper and proxy ordering problems, and is stable.

## Autoscaling
| Layer | Tool | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Pods (horizontal) | HPA on CPU, memory or custom metrics | Needs requests set; v2 supports tolerances and multiple metrics |
| Pods (event-driven) | KEDA | Scale on queue depth, Kafka lag, cron; can scale to zero |
| Pods (vertical) | VPA, or in-place resize | Right-sizes requests; avoid mixing VPA and HPA on the same metric |
| Nodes | Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter | Karpenter provisions right-sized instances directly and consolidates idle nodes |

## Storage and stateful workloads
A **PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)** requests storage; a **StorageClass** says how to provision it (EBS gp3, Azure Disk). A **StatefulSet** gives each replica a stable name (`db-0`, `db-1`) and its own PVC that survives rescheduling. Remember a disk is usually tied to one availability zone, so the Pod must run in that zone. For databases, prefer a managed service or a mature operator (CloudNativePG for Postgres) and test restores, not just backups.

## Security essentials
- **RBAC:** grant least-privilege Roles to ServiceAccounts, not people sharing `cluster-admin`. Give each workload its own ServiceAccount and disable token auto-mount if it never calls the API.
- **Secrets** are base64-encoded, not encrypted, in the API by default. Enable encryption at rest at the API server and sync real secrets from a manager (External Secrets Operator, Secrets Store CSI driver for Key Vault or Secrets Manager) rather than committing them to Git.
- **Pod Security Standards:** enforce the `restricted` profile per namespace (non-root, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities, seccomp runtime default).
- **NetworkPolicy:** the default is allow-all between Pods. Start from default-deny and open only required paths (needs a CNI that enforces it, such as Cilium or Calico).
- **Images:** pin by digest, scan in CI, and run from a private registry with admission checks.

## Packaging and delivery
**Helm** packages templated manifests as versioned charts with values per environment; **Kustomize** patches plain YAML with overlays and ships in `kubectl`. Many teams use Helm for third-party software and Kustomize or Helm for their own. Pair either with **GitOps** (Argo CD or Flux): Git is the desired state and a controller reconciles the cluster to it, which gives review, history and rollback by `git revert`. For traffic in, the Kubernetes project retired the community **Ingress NGINX** controller in March 2026, so new work should use **Gateway API** (`Gateway` and `HTTPRoute`) with a maintained implementation, and existing clusters should plan a migration.

## Worked example: a production-shaped Deployment and PDB
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 }
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: api } }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/api@sha256:<digest>
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
            limits: { memory: 256Mi }
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 5 }
          livenessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /live, port: 8080 }, periodSeconds: 10, failureThreshold: 3 }
          lifecycle: { preStop: { exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] } } }
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: { name: api }
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: api } }
```

## Debugging runbook
| Symptom | First commands | Usual cause |
|---|---|---|
| Pending | `kubectl describe pod`, events | Not enough CPU or memory, taint, unbound PVC, quota |
| CrashLoopBackOff | `kubectl logs --previous`, `describe` | App error, bad config or secret, failing liveness probe |
| OOMKilled (137) | `describe pod` (last state), `kubectl top pod` | Memory limit too low or a leak |
| ImagePullBackOff | `describe pod` | Wrong tag, missing registry credentials |
| Running but unreachable | `kubectl get endpoints`, port-forward to the Pod | Selector mismatch, failing readiness probe, NetworkPolicy |
| Cannot get a shell in a distroless image | `kubectl debug -it pod/x --image=busybox --target=app` | Use an ephemeral debug container |

> [!pitfall] Liveness probes that depend on downstream services. When the dependency fails, Kubernetes restarts healthy Pods and makes the outage worse. Keep liveness local and cheap; use readiness for dependency health.
> [!pitfall] No PDB and no topology spread, then a node upgrade. All replicas can sit on one node and be drained together.
> [!pitfall] Using `latest` tags or mutable tags. Rollbacks and audits become guesswork; pin digests.
> [!cost] Over-requesting is the biggest hidden bill: the cluster pays for reserved requests, not usage. Review requests against real usage monthly and let Karpenter or the Cluster Autoscaler consolidate nodes.
> [!security] Do not mount the Docker or containerd socket, run privileged Pods, or use `hostPath` volumes casually. Each is a path from one compromised container to the node and every Secret on it.
> [!version] Verified 2026-10-19: Kubernetes 1.36 was released on April 22, 2026; in-place Pod resize reached stable in 1.35; and the community Ingress NGINX controller has been retired since March 2026, with Gateway API the recommended path. Managed services lag upstream by months, so check your provider's supported versions.
q: A container exceeds its memory limit and its CPU limit. What happens in each case?
Exceeding the memory limit gets the container OOM-killed (exit 137). Exceeding the CPU limit only throttles it, adding latency.
Why do you need a PodDisruptionBudget even if you run three replicas?
Voluntary disruptions like node drains can evict replicas simultaneously; a PDB keeps a minimum number available during upgrades and scale-downs.
Why should a liveness probe avoid checking the database?
If the database is briefly down, every Pod fails liveness and is restarted, turning a dependency blip into a full outage. Use readiness for dependency checks.
